newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore court orders ex-Merrill man to return.
newsitem.headline: Singapore court orders ex-Merrill man to return.

text.p: Singapore's High Court has ordered former Merrill Lynch banker Kevin Wallace to return to the island for questioning over assets he declared to the court, a lawyer close to the case said on Tuesday.
Wallace has been charged with money laundering and Merrill's lawyers won a court order to place his assets and those of his wife under receivership.
"There was an open court hearing yesterday on very short notice," the lawyer told Reuters.
Wallace's lawyers in Hong Kong, however, were applying on Tuesday to discharge a similar injunction against him there, and no date was set for his return to Singapore.
"At the moment he cannot leave Hong Kong because of the High Court order prohibiting him from doing it, and because of the bail," he said.
"If he applies there in Hong Kong and the court says he cannot leave, he will be cross-examined in Hong Kong," he said.
Wallace, a 46-year-old American, was charged in Hong Kong with money laundering and is free on bail of more than HK$1 million.

Merrill Lynch started civil proceedings against Wallace in Singapore and Hong Kong in June. Within a week, Merrill lawyers won various orders against Wallace, including an injunction to freeze US$15 million of his assets worldwide.
They also succeeded in getting an order to include his wife's assets in actions against him, the lawyer said.
The bank accused him of engaging in unauthorised trading, misrepresenting or falsifying private clients' statements and forging client signatures.
Wallace was a financial consultant to wealthy clients across Asia while employed by Merrill from late 1991 until his dismissal on May 15 this year.
Industry sources have said his clients were believed to have bank balances of up to US$25 million.
Legal sources said a Singapore court order could effectively put aside "weak" criminal charges against Wallace in Hong Kong.
It also serves to get around the extradition treaty between Singapore and Hong Kong, an agreement that some experts say might have lapsed when the territory was returned to China on July 1.
Singapore's white collar crime bureau, the Commercial Affairs Department, has said it was investigating allegations against Wallace but had not yet brought charges.

Accounting firm Arthur Anderson, the appointed receivers, will start examining a list of Wallace's assets. The court ordered DBS Bank and OCBC Bank to provide Merrill with details of Wallace's bank accounts.
A Merrill spokesman in Hong Kong could not be immediately reached for comment.
